units: the price of a handmade piece of furniture comes from several sources
the raw material bought from the supplier counts toward the total
the joiner's tools wear down and have to be replaced
the solid wood bench used for shaping deteriorates with use
the craftsman's hand is acquired through long practice
the beginner copies that hand imperfectly
the customer's wait matches a stretch with no money coming in
no single one of these sources justifies the sum asked on its own
text: Walk into a joiner's workshop and the price of a finished piece turns out to come from many places at once, each worth naming on its own. Start with the material: timber chosen, dried, and paid for at the supplier's counter. Then the tools, the planes and clamps that lose their edge and have to be swapped out. Then the bench itself, a heavy slab of solid wood that wears away season after season while nobody thinks about it. Then the hand of the craftsman, slow to acquire, and the hand of the beginner still copying it clumsily. Then the waiting, the stretch of time a buyer sits through while nothing comes into the till. Not one of these sources, taken alone, explains the sum on the label. A buyer who calls it steep sees a smooth board. The maker sees the whole chain of spending behind it.

units: the head of the crew kept a record of operations
the foundations advanced on schedule during the first week
a steel delivery arrived incomplete the following week
the load calculations had to be redone beam by beam
the supplier blamed a break in supply
an engineer offered to replace the section with an equivalent one held in stock
the substitution was approved on condition that the slab be strengthened
output dropped before settling again
the extra cost showed up on the final invoice
text: The site foreman opened his logbook on the first morning of the job and set down the order of operations. Through the opening week the foundations went up on schedule, and the crews rotated without a hitch. The week after, a steel delivery turned up short, so the load calculations had to be redone beam by beam. The supplier blamed a break in his own supply, which the client refused to swallow without applying a contractual penalty. A technical meeting was called, and the structural engineer offered to swap in an equivalent section already sitting in stock. The substitution cleared review on one condition: the topping slab had to be thickened. When work resumed, output fell a notch, then held steady. The logbook kept the trace of that gap, and the final invoice turned it into an overrun.

units: a written estimate must be requested before any repair starts
an agreement made only in speech protects neither side
the document must state the work, the materials and the time announced
money paid in advance binds the customer to the contractor
the contractor cannot keep that advance if the work never began
proofs of payment form the basis of a claim
any change decided while work is under way must be notified in writing
the final bill must be set against the accepted estimate point by point
text: Before any sizeable repair begins, ask for a written estimate, because a spoken agreement leaves neither side protected once a quarrel starts. The document should spell out what will be done, which materials go in, and how long the work is announced to take. Read the deposit clause closely. Money paid up front binds you to the contractor, and the contractor has no right to keep it if the job never started. Hold on to every proof of payment, since that is what a claim will rest on later. Put any change agreed while the work is under way in writing, or the closing bill will climb above the first estimate and leave you no recourse. Last of all, set the bill you receive against the estimate you accepted, point by point. A gap with no reason behind it is fair grounds for refusing to pay.

units: a storage building has been running slowly since it lost its main client
orders have dropped sharply
part of the staff has moved to reduced hours
seasonal hiring has been halted
the freight companies nearby fear the consequences
sharing the building among several shippers is being considered
converting the floor space requires automated sorting equipment
the local council would pay for half of that equipment
a first occupant is said to have signed a promise to lease
text: A storage building on the freight park has been running at half speed since it lost its main client. Managers describe a sharp fall in orders that has emptied the loading bays and left the forklifts standing. Part of the staff has moved onto reduced hours, and the seasonal hiring that usually starts about now was called off. Freight companies nearby fear the knock-on effect, since their runs have already thinned. One idea is on the table: share the building among several mid-sized shippers instead of hanging everything on a single customer. Management points out that converting the floor space calls for automated sorting equipment, half of it paid for by the local council. A first occupant is said to have signed a promise to lease, which would reopen hiring in time for the busy season.

units: the two aisles of the covered market do not run at the same pace
the fruit seller calls out to passers-by and announces his prices aloud
he drops a price as soon as goods risk spoiling
the cheese shop ages its products in a cellar
its posted prices seldom change
perishable goods force a sale in a hurry
a product that improves with age allows waiting
the first business takes on seasonal hands during the glut
the second keeps the same employee all year
text: Take a look at the two aisles of the covered market, because they do not run on the same clock at all. Down the first one the fruit stall spills over with crates. The seller calls out to anyone walking past, shouts his prices across the aisle, and drops one the moment a crate looks ready to turn. Down the second, the cheese shop ages its stock in a cellar, keeps its labels quiet, and hardly ever moves a figure. The first man sells freshness, so he lives in a hurry. The second sells patience, so he can wait for his buyer. You will notice too that one takes on extra hands when the harvest pours in, while the other keeps the same employee all year round. Two shops side by side, two opposite ways of earning a living. The goods set the pace, and the pace decides the takings.

units: the argument over funding social protection overlooks three aspects
the deduction from wages is felt as a tax imposed from outside
that deduction in fact pays for shared cover
the uneven earnings of the self-employed make any fixed scale unfair
the protection of the self-employed remains incomplete
some employers escape the deductions by using short contracts
farming assignments out to others feeds the same avoidance
the writer holds that the matter belongs to fairness and not to bookkeeping
text: Three blind spots hang over the argument about how social protection gets paid for, and they are seldom raised together. The first is the contribution itself. Taken straight out of wages, it looks like a tax imposed from above, when what it actually buys is shared cover. The second concerns the self-employed, whose earnings arrive unevenly, which makes any fixed scale unfair, and whose protection is still full of holes. The third is the quietest: employers who slip out of paying by stacking up short contracts and farming assignments out to others. Each of these leads back to a question of fairness rather than bookkeeping. Those calling for across-the-board relief dodge the first. Those defending things as they stand dodge the third. The argument would gain from naming all three before anyone settles it.

units: the oldest hand in the bindery came in very young as a trainee
she was put first on cleaning and then on folding the gatherings
mixing the glues was handed to her after that
she spent long seasons at the same shaping bench
she bought out the client list when the house nearly disappeared
that buyout was paid for with her savings and two loans
she trained about a dozen young people
several of her pupils now run shops of their own
she handed the business to her last pupil, asking her not to sell the work cheap
text: The oldest hand in the bindery came in very young, as a trainee, back when the leather was still sewn entirely by hand. They gave her the sweeping first, then the folding of the gatherings, and a season later the mixing of the glues. She spent long seasons at the same shaping bench, whose worn top still carries the marks left by her tools. When the house came close to going under, she bought out the client list with her own savings and two modest loans. After that she trained a dozen young people, several of whom now run shops of their own. Too tired at last to work the press, she handed the business over to her final pupil, asking her one thing only: never sell the work cheap. She still comes in to sit by the window, and puts a word to a stitch that has been pulled loose.

units: the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line draws a mixed verdict
the tightening is controlled electronically and its accuracy is beyond dispute
that accuracy does away with the rework caused by tightening by hand
the machine now sets the pace for the operator
a badly seated part locks the station and blocks the ones before it
the workshop has gained in steadiness and lost in flexibility
upkeep calls for electronics skills the team does not have
every breakdown means waiting for an outside technician
the share of faulty parts has fallen markedly
text: The equipment recently fitted to the assembly line deserves a mixed verdict. Its tightening accuracy is beyond dispute, since the torque is controlled electronically, which does away with the rework that tightening by hand used to cause. That accuracy, though, brings a pace set by the machine rather than by the operator. Because the cycle no longer pauses, one badly seated part locks up the whole station and the stoppage travels back down the line. What the workshop has gained in steadiness it has lost in flexibility. A less visible effect comes with it: upkeep now calls for electronics skills the team does not have, so every breakdown ends in waiting for an outside technician. The balance still tips the right way, because faulty parts have grown much rarer. Operators ought to be trained to read common faults themselves.

units: the writer ordered a kitchen and signed a detailed estimate
a deposit was paid when the order was placed
no word about delivery has come since
three dates in a row were announced and then missed
the writer's last message went unanswered
the writer has to rent a furnished home, which raises his expenses
he asks either for a written commitment to a firm date with compensation
or else for the deposit to be returned in full within two weeks
he states that the file will go to a consumer association if no agreement is reached
text: I am writing to you once more about the kitchen I ordered from your showroom at the start of the season. I signed a detailed estimate and paid the deposit you asked for, and since then not one word about delivery has reached me. Your advisers have named three delivery dates in turn, every one of them missed, and my last message has gone unanswered. Because of this I am having to rent a furnished place of my own, which adds to my expenses week after week. Let me put a reasonable way out of this to you. Either you commit in writing to a firm installation date, with a reduction covering what the wait has cost me, or you return the deposit in full within two weeks. Failing an agreement, I will hand the file to the consumer association already following my case. I look forward to your reply.

units: the choice between an employee and an outside contractor comes up often in small firms
the contractor's invoice takes the place of a wage and the employer's charges
the contractor looks cheaper in the short run
the contractor bills for each job separately
the employee takes on unplanned work at no extra charge
the training an employee receives then serves the firm that paid for it
an exclusive, long-running tie with a contractor risks being reclassified
the advice is to keep service contracts for one-off, specialized needs
the advice is to hire for the core activity
text: Is it better to hire an employee or bring in an outside contractor? The question comes up again and again in small firms, and the answer depends on what you are measuring. On immediate cost the contractor looks cheaper, since one invoice takes the place of a wage plus the employer's charges. Over time the gap narrows: the contractor bills for each job separately, while an employee soaks up the unplanned work at no extra charge. And loyalty? That leans clearly toward hiring, because the training an employee receives goes on serving the firm that paid for it. Legal risk runs the other way. An exclusive, long-running tie with a contractor can be reclassified. So what should you choose? Keep service contracts for one-off, specialized needs, and hire for whatever sits at the heart of the business.
